message:
Before you answer, a reminder of how we work:

1. Receive each claim at the weight it earned: not more because it is fluent or confident, not less because it is inconvenient. Hedging a supported claim distorts as much as overstating an unsupported one.
2. Take in what was said before you answer. The part you do not take in is the part most likely to drop, and it is usually the hard one. Then move.
3. Go to the source. Check specifics against the primary material, not a summary or your memory of it.
4. Do not close what is open, and do not keep open what is closed. Say which is which, and what would settle an open question.
5. Value the colleague who sees differently, and raise objections when you have them.
6. Make your moves where they can be seen.
7. Failures come in pairs. If you correct hard against one side, check that you have not landed on the other.

---

Please review the following document.

Here is how its author describes it:

<author>
This proposal is built on our own trading history, not just competitor benchmarking, and that is what makes me confident in it. The key question with any rate rise is price sensitivity, and we have a direct test: when we raised the weekend rate by £10 last June, weekend occupancy went up, from 81% to 89%, the following month. Combined with a value-for-money score of 8.4, the best in our set, and rates £20 to £35 below competitors, everything points the same way. The revenue estimate is deliberately conservative: it assumes no occupancy gain and puts no value at all on the extra Friday and Sunday nights that the two-night minimum will generate, so £204,000 is a floor rather than a target. We have also built in a clear monitoring trigger, so if occupancy does dip we will see it within a month and can respond. Corporate and group commitments are protected. I think this is a well-evidenced, low-risk change that brings our pricing into line with the quality of the hotel.
</author>

<document>
Pricing Proposal: Weekend Rate Restructure
Harbourside Hotel, Revenue Management, April 2026

1. Proposal
From 1 June 2026 we propose to (a) raise the Best Available Rate (BAR) for Friday and Saturday nights from £145 to £165, and (b) introduce a two-night minimum for any stay that includes a Saturday night. Midweek rates are unchanged.

2. Context
Harbourside is a 112-room four-star hotel on the quay, with a leisure-led weekend business and a corporate-led midweek business. Our weekend BAR is £20 to £35 below the three comparable hotels in our competitive set, whose weekend rates currently range from £165 to £180. Weekend occupancy has recovered strongly since 2023 and we believe we are leaving money on the table.

Table 1. Weekend (Friday and Saturday) occupancy by month, 2025
Jan 62% | Feb 66% | Mar 74% | Apr 80% | May 85% | Jun 81%
Jul 89% | Aug 93% | Sep 88% | Oct 82% | Nov 72% | Dec 78%

Average weekend occupancy across 2025 was 79%. July and August are our strongest months, driven by the harbour festival and the school summer holidays, with September also benefiting from late-season visitors.

3. Evidence on price sensitivity
In the last week of June 2025 we raised the weekend BAR by £10, from £135 to the current £145. Weekend occupancy in July rose to 89%, from 81% in June. This tells us that our weekend guests are not price sensitive at current levels; if anything, the higher rate appears to have reinforced our positioning as a quality option, and we expect the further increase to be absorbed in the same way.

This is consistent with feedback from our guest satisfaction surveys, where weekend guests rate "value for money" at 8.4 out of 10, the highest score among our competitive set.

4. Two-night minimum
Saturday nights are our most constrained inventory: we sold out on 31 Saturdays in 2025. Many of these guests stay only one night, leaving rooms empty on Friday or Sunday either side. A two-night minimum for stays including a Saturday will convert single-night Saturday stays into two-night stays and smooth occupancy across the weekend.

Our booking data show that weddings at Quayside Hall, the venue next door, account for around 38% of our Saturday-night room bookings. Wedding guests typically book as a block through the couple, arrive on the Saturday afternoon and check out on the Sunday morning.

5. Revenue impact
Across our 124 rooms, 104 weekend nights a year and average weekend occupancy of 79%, a £20 increase in BAR is worth about £204,000 a year in additional room revenue, before any gain from longer stays. We have assumed weekend occupancy is maintained at 2025 levels, which we consider prudent given the evidence above.

The two-night minimum should add further revenue through additional Friday and Sunday nights. We have not quantified this but expect it to be material, particularly in shoulder months.

6. Implementation and monitoring
The new rates will be loaded into the channel manager on 15 May for stays from 1 June, giving online travel agencies two weeks' notice. Corporate contracted rates and group rates already contracted will be honoured. We will review pick-up weekly against the same weeks in 2025 and report to the General Manager monthly. If weekend occupancy for any month falls more than five points below 2025, we will review the rate.

7. Recommendation
The evidence shows that our weekend guests are not price sensitive at current rates and that we are priced well below our competitive set. We recommend approval of the £165 weekend BAR and the two-night Saturday minimum from 1 June 2026, delivering at least £204,000 of additional annual room revenue.
</document>
response:
# Review of the Harbourside Hotel Weekend Rate Restructure

**Overall:** A weekend rate rise is probably justified. But the document's own data supports it better than the evidence it cites. The 31 sold-out Saturdays are genuine evidence that demand exceeds supply. The June-to-July "test" is not evidence of anything.

The proposal has three serious problems:
- the revenue figure is overstated;
- the two-night minimum puts the hotel's largest single source of Saturday business at risk;
- "£204,000 is a floor" is not true.

Of the author's main claims:
- **Hold up:** the arithmetic, the 79% average, the competitive gap, and the five-point trigger as a rate safeguard.
- **Do not:** "a direct test" of price sensitivity, "deliberately conservative," "a floor," and "low-risk."

## What checks out

- **Average occupancy.** Table 1 averages 79.2%, as stated.
- **The £204,000 figure.** The arithmetic is right on the inputs given: 124 × 104 × 0.79 × £20 = £203,757.
- **The competitive gap.** At £145 the hotel is £20–£35 below a set priced £165–£180. At £165 it would match the cheapest competitor, so "in line with" the set is a fair description.
- **The five-point trigger.** It is sound as a safeguard on the rate itself. A 13.8% price rise only loses revenue if occupancy falls by about 12% in relative terms, which is roughly 9–10 points at current levels. A five-point trigger therefore fires well before the rate rise starts costing money.

## Main problems

### 1. The June–July comparison is seasonality, not price insensitivity

The document's own Table 1 and commentary say July and August are the strongest months because of the harbour festival and school holidays. Occupancy would have risen from June to July whatever the rate did.

The comparison says nothing about how guests respond to price. "If anything, the higher rate appears to have reinforced our positioning" has no support at all.

**This question is open, and the hotel can settle it from its own records.** Compare July–December 2025 at £145 with the same months of 2024 at £135, allowing for market-wide movement. Competitor or STR benchmark occupancy would provide that control.

The value-for-money score (8.4) is weaker support than it looks. It was measured at the lowest price in the set, and it will likely fall when the price rises. It suggests some headroom, but it can't show that guests won't respond to a £20 increase.

### 2. The revenue figure is overstated

**Room count.** Section 2 says the hotel has **112 rooms**. Section 5 calculates on **124**. Using 112 gives £184,000.

**Who actually pays BAR.** The £20 applies only to rooms sold at BAR. Contracted corporate and group rates are honoured, and weddings make up about 38% of Saturday-night bookings, typically block-booked through the couple. If those blocks are on group rates, they won't pay the higher BAR. Friday's mix isn't given. Excluding wedding blocks on Saturdays alone removes about 19% of weekend room-nights, bringing the figure to about £149,000.

**VAT.** This applies if rates are quoted VAT-inclusive, as is usual for UK leisure rates. A £20 rise then brings in about £16.67 of room revenue, giving roughly **£124,000**.

**OTA commission.** Online travel agencies typically take 15–20% on the bookings they deliver, which lowers the net figure further.

**Year one.** Reservations made before 15 May for June onwards will be honoured at £145, so first-year revenue is lower still.

**Realistic figure:** roughly **£100,000–£125,000 a year**, before any change in occupancy. That is about half the stated figure.

### 3. The two-night minimum threatens 38% of Saturday business

The document says wedding guests arrive on the Saturday and leave on the Sunday morning. They are exactly the one-night Saturday stays the minimum would block. Only *already contracted* group rates are protected, so future wedding blocks would fall under the rule.

Wedding guests come for one night because the wedding is one night. Most will not book two. They will go to other hotels or short-term lets. That puts at risk:
- a large share of Saturday occupancy;
- the relationship with Quayside Hall.

The minimum also behaves differently on different Saturdays:
- **The 31 sold-out Saturdays.** The minimum can work here, if enough two-night demand exists to replace the one-night stays it displaces.
- **The other 21 Saturdays.** The rule simply turns away one-night guests the hotel had room for.

So the two-night minimum carries real downside, not just unquantified upside. **Wedding and other group blocks need an explicit exemption.** Even with one, the rule should probably be limited to Saturdays forecast to sell out.

### 4. The revenue figure is not a floor

The author calls the estimate conservative because "it assumes no occupancy gain." But a price rise is not expected to *raise* occupancy. Holding occupancy flat is a central, arguably optimistic, assumption, not a cautious one.

The one element left unquantified, the two-night minimum, has a downside as well as an upside. Together with point 2, that means **£204,000 is an overstatement, not a floor.**

### 5. Monitoring will be slower than the author expects

The author says "we will see it within a month." But reservations already made at £145 will fill June and probably part of July. Wedding blocks are booked months ahead. So monthly occupancy will mostly reflect old bookings for some time.

The weekly pick-up review against 2025 is the right early signal. To make it useful:
- track it separately by segment (BAR, groups, weddings);
- track it separately by night (Friday, Saturday);
- set the trigger on pace for future dates, not on a month's actual occupancy.

## What the evidence does support

The strongest case in the document is one it barely uses. Selling out on **31 Saturdays** shows Saturday demand exceeds supply at £145. A higher Saturday rate is well supported. Friday is less clear, because Friday occupancy isn't reported separately, and weekend figures blend the two nights.

## Suggested changes before approval

1. Settle the room count, then restate the estimate to cover BAR-only room-nights, net of VAT and commission, with the first-year reduction shown separately.
2. Remove "floor" and "conservative." Give a central estimate with an occupancy-loss sensitivity: revenue is neutral at about a 12% relative drop in occupancy.
3. Replace the June–July evidence with a year-on-year comparison of July–December 2025 against 2024.
4. Exempt wedding and group blocks from the two-night minimum. Consider applying it only to forecast sell-out Saturdays.
5. Report Friday and Saturday occupancy separately, and consider a larger rise on Saturday than on Friday.
6. Move the monitoring trigger from monthly occupancy to weekly pace, by segment.
